extracted.intended_audience: students and beginning researchers learning to do and report research (undergraduate/early_graduate)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for planning, conducting, and writing research reports that answer a clear question and meet readers' expectations across academic and practical communities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trustworthy reporting / accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: We trust research only because we think it was done carefully and reported accurately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reliable publication, careful methods, accurate reporting, and the testing role of editors/reviewers/skeptical readers are what make research believable. Without trustworthy published research we'd be prisoners of immediate opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amiable skepticism toward sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Be amiably skeptical of the research you read, to question it even as you realize how much you depend on it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Question reports while recognizing dependence on published work; do not accept findings uncritically. The text urges continual critical evaluation of others' research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research answers a question that solves a problem
rubrics_metrics.description: We do research whenever we gather information to answer a question that solves a problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame research as a problem-to-be-solved (examples: finding a part, checking a birth date, discovering a species). This framing guides appropriate methods and reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write to remember (note-taking)
rubrics_metrics.description: Experienced researchers first write just to remember what they've read.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take notes to avoid forgetting or misremembering sources and claims. Routine note-taking prevents errors in later drafts and helps accurate citation and synthesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write to understand (organizing and seeing patterns)
rubrics_metrics.description: Write to see larger patterns in what you read; arranging results in different ways reveals new implications, connections, and complications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use outlines, rearrangements, diagrams, and comparisons of sources to discover contradictions, ignored evidence, or opportunities for synthesis. Don't postpone writing until all data are gathered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write to test your thinking
rubrics_metrics.description: Get thoughts out of your head and onto paper to see whether ideas are as compelling as they seemed mentally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drafts reveal weaknesses; writing early in the project helps evaluate ideas objectively and improves both thinking and reading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipate readers' critical questions
rubrics_metrics.description: When you write for others, imagine and meet readers' inevitable and critical questions: How have you evaluated your evidence? Why do you think it's relevant? What ideas have you considered but rejected?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design the report to answer these predictable questions. Failure to do so often reveals flaws in reasoning or insufficient evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt community-standard forms and conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Report your research as the members of your intended community do; standard forms evolved to help writers question their thinking and embody shared values.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn and use the formats, terminology, citation practices, and rhetorical forms expected by your intended readers so you can answer their predictable questions and be understood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create an appropriate role for yourself and readers
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide before writing what role you will play (expert, colleague, explainer) and what role you will cast your readers in, because those roles become fixed in writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selecting the wrong persona (e.g., overly technical for novices or patronizing for experts) leads to losing readers. Use examples (passages ia vs ib) to match tone and technicality to reader knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid the 'data-grubbing/student-as-handyman' stance
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't write as if your role is just to show how many facts you can dig up for a teacher who will grade you; that demeans you and wastes the opportunity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instead, present findings as contributions: new facts, solutions to problems, or answers to important questions — and justify why readers should care.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select the researcher role that fits your goals (three roles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose whether your report's primary value is: 1) I've found some new and interesting information; 2) I've found a solution to an important practical problem; 3) I've found an answer to an important question (scholarly understanding).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each role requires different evidence, tone, and audience expectations. For example, applied/practical reports require relevant facts and credibility; scholarly reports demand objectivity and situating findings within literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imagine and motivate the reader's role (social contract)
rubrics_metrics.description: Offer readers a social contract: I'll play my part if you play yours — imagine what they will accept and what they are willing to do (listen, judge, act).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design your report to motivate readers to adopt the role you need (entertained, informed, or able to act). Miscasting readers risks losing them entirely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match evidence type to readers' expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine the kind of evidence your readers will expect: primary vs secondary sources, quantitative data vs quotations, firsthand observations, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before committing to a topic, decide whether readers will accept the data you can collect. Use the right evidence for the community and the question asked.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure availability and sufficiency of data
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether you can find the data your readers will expect. If you don't have data you can use as evidence, you haven't collected enough.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not start a project without verifying you can obtain the necessary primary or secondary sources; plan for evidence gathering and possible topic refinement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be feasible and specific in topic selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Find a topic specific enough to let you master a reasonable amount of information in the time you have (examples given).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid overly broad topics; choose narrow, researchable topics (e.g., specific journals, plays, dates) so you can gather adequate evidence and produce a coherent report.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write throughout research (writing-as-research)
rubrics_metrics.description: Resolve to do lots of writing along the way — notes, outlines, reflective writing, diagrams, and journaling — to encourage critical thinking and discovery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many of these writings won't appear in the final draft, but they are essential for understanding sources, developing arguments, and productive drafting later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use peer feedback and writing groups
rubrics_metrics.description: Form or join a writing group to discuss progress, summarize projects concisely, review outlines and drafts, and impose discipline and schedule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Groups are valuable for discipline, feedback on readers' reactions, brainstorming, and catching problems that future readers will see. Meet regularly and present elevator summaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: For applied reports: practical relevance and credibility
rubrics_metrics.description: When writing to solve a practical problem, use the right terminology, cite reliable sources, find and present the right evidence in the right format, and design the report around the specific intention to advise a decision maker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select only the evidence relevant to solving the practical problem and show its reliability so decision-makers can act on your advice.

rubrics_metrics.name: For scholarly audiences: objectivity, rigorous logic, and evidential relevance
rubrics_metrics.description: Academic readers expect objectivity, rigorous logic, examination of issues from all sides, well-documented facts, and demonstration of how new data improve understanding of an important scholarly question.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nail down facts, anticipate challenges to authenticity or relevance, and situate new evidence in terms of its contribution to the scholarly conversation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Checklist for understanding readers (audience analysis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Answer early and revisit: Who will read my report? What do they expect me to do (entertain, inform, solve practical problem)? How much do they already know? How will they respond to my main claim?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these questions to plan tone, evidence, explanations, and the level of detail. Reassess when planning and revising. Anticipate contradictions with readers' beliefs and standard counterarguments.
